The core innovation lies in transferring NFL route classification methodologies to soccer through a shared temporal and kinematic framework. The method begins by extracting three key features—distance, angle, and speed—from NGS data within a 3.0-second window post-snap. These features form a 93-dimensional vector space (31 frames × 3 features) that captures the spatial and dynamic evolution of player movements. A Random Forest classifier is then trained on this feature set using 2161 labeled NFL routes, enabling it to generalize to soccer runs. The alignment of soccer events to 'soccer snaps' ensures temporal consistency across datasets. This approach leverages the structured labeling of NFL routes to infer categorical structure in soccer, despite the absence of such annotations. The model's performance, with 73% accuracy, reflects its ability to capture recurring movement patterns but also highlights limitations in handling less frequent or ambiguous runs. The framework thus establishes a dual-layered abstraction: one grounded in physical motion and another in categorical semantics, bridging two distinct sports domains.
